messages.content:
Assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category. Here are worked examples, then the case to code.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: I21

Example 3
Hospital course: A 34-year-old woman presented with fever, rigors, dysuria and right flank tenderness. Urine microscopy showed pyuria and culture grew Escherichia coli. Computed tomography showed a swollen right kidney with no abscess. She improved on intravenous ceftriaxone.
Answer: N10

Example 4
Hospital course: An 81-year-old woman was brought in after a fall at home. She could not weight-bear and the right leg was shortened and externally rotated. A pelvic radiograph showed a displaced subcapital fracture of the right femoral neck. She underwent hemiarthroplasty on day one.
Answer: S72

Example 5
Hospital course: A 19-year-old man presented with 18 hours of periumbilical pain that migrated to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia and a low-grade fever. There was guarding at McBurney's point and the white cell count was 15.2. Laparoscopy confirmed an inflamed, non-perforated appendix.
Answer: K35

Example 6
Hospital course: A 64-year-old woman with a history of oestrogen-receptor-positive breast carcinoma treated five years earlier presented with progressive thoracic back pain. Magnetic resonance imaging showed deposits in T7 and T9 with no cord compression. Biopsy confirmed deposits of breast origin and she received palliative radiotherapy to the spine.
Answer: C79

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary

Patient Information:
Name: Anonymous
Gender: Female
Age: 25
Admission Date: [date]
Discharge Date: [date]
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
The patient was administered with various medications including alprazolam 500 μg, duloxetine 90 mg, olanzapine 5 mg, haloperidol 2.5 mg, clonazepam, baclofen, diazepam, phenytoin, levetiracetam, lamotrigine, levodopa, oral baclofen, lacosamide and potassium channel antagonist 3,4 diaminopyridine.

Hospital Course:
The patient was admitted with vomiting, bilateral leg pain, difficulty mobilising and flexed posture of her neck. She later developed visual and auditory hallucinations, respiratory failure with a coma scale score of 3, hypertensive, tachycardic, pyrexic and severe limb rigidity. Subsequently, contractures of the hands and feet were also developed. The patient was intubated and ventilated. The patient intermittently reported visual hallucinations throughout the hospital admission. Further complications included ileus, ischaemic bowel and sepsis.

Outcome:
The patient showed marked clinical improvement with the administration of potassium channel antagonist 3,4 diaminopyridine. This resulted in extubation, multiple medication decreases, transfer from ICU, and ultimately discharged home sixteen months after admission. The patient is now dependent on others for all activities of daily living and has developed contractures of the upper and lower limbs. There have been no documented seizures since discharge.

Follow-up:
The patient requires long-term follow-up care for contractures of the upper and lower limbs. The patient may also benefit from genetic counselling and additional investigations as advised by the neurology team.

Answer with the three-character category only.

text:
This presentation suggests a stiff-person-spectrum or neuromyotonia-like disorder: severe rigidity, contractures, hallucinations, autonomic instability, and respiratory failure. It improved markedly with 3,4-diaminopyridine, a potassium channel blocker. That response, along with the mention of genetic counselling, points toward a channelopathy or a hyperexcitability syndrome.

Several candidate diagnoses fit parts of the picture:
- Isaacs syndrome (neuromyotonia) is coded G71.1 in ICD-10-AM, myotonic disorders.
- Stiff-person syndrome is G25.8 in ICD-10, in the category G25 (other extrapyramidal and movement disorders).
- Morvan syndrome is a CASPR2-related condition combining neuromyotonia, autonomic features and hallucinations or encephalopathy. It is typically coded G71.1 or G73.
- Autoimmune encephalitis would be G04.8 or G04.
- Hyperekplexia would be G25 or similar.

Morvan syndrome fits best: hallucinations, autonomic instability, rigidity, and a response to potassium channel blockade. The rigidity and flexed neck posture could also suggest stiff-person syndrome. However, 3,4-DAP is typically used for Lambert-Eaton syndrome (G70.8 or G73.1) and for potassium channel conditions.

The genetic counselling comment suggests the diagnosis may be a genetic one, possibly a channelopathy such as a KCNA1 variant (episodic ataxia) or a condition related to the prolonged contractures. The withheld diagnosis could also be an unusual one such as a neurodegeneration disorder.

Weighing these, I'll go with neuromyotonia/Morvan-type presentation, coded as G71.

**G71**
